SBI2 CytoData hackathon, November 2026. Altair team: cell-cycle state in image-based screens.

Is It Just the Cell Cycle?

Cells that carry the same genetic perturbation still look very different from one another. Part of that is where each cell is in its division cycle.

We asked two things. Can we read the cell cycle from label-free phase-contrast images? And if we remove it, do perturbed cell populations become more alike? The first answer is yes. The second is: only a little. The cycle explains a few percent of single-cell variation, and knockout phenotypes are mostly something else.

1A cell's place in its cycle changes how it looks

Optical pooled screens image hundreds of thousands of cells, each carrying one CRISPR knockout. If a knockout changes how many cells sit at each cycle stage, its image profile mixes two things: "this gene changes the cycle" and "this gene changes the cell".

The cell cycle in one line. A cell grows with one copy of its genome (G1, called 2N), copies its DNA (S), holds two copies (G2, called 4N) and divides (mitosis), giving two G1 cells. Size, DNA amount and nuclear shape all change along the way.

The hackathon goal. Use measured ground truth (proteins, DNA, RNA) to learn a cell-cycle readout from images, then remove it from perturbation profiles and test whether perturbed populations become less heterogeneous.

Why it matters. If the cycle drives much of the spread, correcting for it would sharpen every phenotype in a screen. If it does not, the cycle is better used as a readout in its own right.

2Three datasets, each with a different ground truth

All three use A549 lung cancer cells. Two measure images and a cell-cycle ground truth in the same cells; the third has RNA averaged per knockout.

The phase-contrast image and the 4i image of each OPS0077 cell are matched by position, so every cell has a label-free view and a measured cycle state.

3We built cell-cycle clocks from the ground truth, then checked what each part contains

A clock turns each cell's markers into a position on a circle. The labels on that circle have to be checked against something measured, because the circle has no natural starting point.

What we did. In OPS0077, Louise fitted a closed curve through DNA content, pRb, p21 and the phosphorylated fraction of Rb, which gives each control cell a position from 0 to 1 (35,633 of 52,220 control cells have all four inputs). Position 0 is the lowest-DNA part of the loop, DNA peaks at about 0.55 to 0.6, and p21 is lowest around S. In Element, a model of the RNA (cycleVI) gives each cell an angle. We then read out the DNA content of the cells at each position.

What we found. The doubled-DNA cells (4N) sit at 0.5 to 0.75, and the last quarter, 0.75 to 1, is almost entirely cells that have just divided and are back to one copy. Labelling the four quarters "Early G1, Late G1, S, G2/M" shifted every label by about a quarter.

Why it matters. This explained a puzzle from the first day. Knockouts expected to stop cells in G1 seemed to pile up in "G2/M" (CDK7 showed +10.8% "G2/M"). Those were G1 cells after division, so the knockouts did what was expected.

4Label-free phase contrast reads the cycle about as well as the antibody panel

Trained on control cells and tested on images it never saw, phase contrast separates 4N from 2N cells with a score of 0.92, against 0.89 for the 4i antibody panel.

What we did. We trained models that predict each cell's measured clock position and DNA state from its phase-contrast features, and scored them on held-out image tiles. Brian's model (gradient-boosted trees on the raw features) was compared with ours (a linear model on 100 principal components) on the same folds.

What we found. Gradient boosting places cells on the clock with a typical error of 22 degrees out of 360, against 29 for the linear model (random guessing gives 90). Louise's independent circular model reaches a mean error of 0.105 turns (38 degrees) on cells it never saw and 0.113 turns on a whole held-out well. It also works on knockout cells: a model trained only on controls separates 4N from 2N in knockout cells as well as in control cells (0.963 against 0.968).

Why it matters. Any screen with brightfield or phase-contrast images can get a cell-cycle readout without spending a fluorescence channel on it.

5Clocks from different datasets only partly line up

Within one dataset the clocks agree. Between the protein-based clock (OPS0077) and the RNA-based clock (Element) only the stretch from DNA copying to division can be matched.

What we did. We rotated and compared the clocks using features measured the same way in both datasets: DNA content, cell and nuclear size, and cell shape.

What we found. The DNA-based OPS0077 clocks agree within 4 to 6 degrees. Across datasets, DNA lines up the S to G2/M arc, but size and shape do not agree on the rotation, and no combination beats a random-rotation control. The G1 part cannot be aligned with what both datasets share.

A second route: transfer a model. A forest trained on Element DNA-stain features (DNA amount, nuclear size and texture) to predict the RNA clock reaches 53 degrees error on held-out Element wells. Applied to OPS0077 cells and compared with their 4i clock, it gets the same quarter for 34.6% of cells (25% by chance). Keeping only the 56 features whose distributions match between the datasets raises this to 49% and lowers the median disagreement from 53.6 to 41.6 degrees. The agreement is again strongest from S to G2.

Why it matters. To compare cell-cycle effects across platforms, use DNA-content classes (2N, S, 4N), which are measured identically, rather than clock angles.

6Phase contrast finds the knockouts that shift the cycle, and a DNA stain confirms them

Across all 1,000 knockouts, the phase-contrast readout flags genes whose cells pile up at a different cycle stage. When we measured DNA directly, the predicted shifts held.

What we did. For every knockout we compared its predicted cycle distribution with control cells, using groups of control cells of the same size as a fair reference. Then we measured DNA content from the DAPI stain in 269 knockouts: the predicted shifters, a random set without a predicted shift, the 60 genes the team expected to cause an arrest, and the extra knockouts only the gradient-boosting model flags.

What we found. The predicted change in 4N cells matches the measured change (rank correlation 0.80 for gradient boosting and 0.74 for the linear model, over 269 knockouts). DNA replication genes gain 4N cells (MTBP +17 points, MCM7 +12, CDC45 +8). Ribosome, proteasome, chaperone and splicing genes lose them, as expected for cells that stall before copying their DNA.

Newest check. Gradient boosting flags 194 knockouts and the linear model 81. We have now measured DNA in every flagged knockout. Of those both models flag, 41 of 73 (56%) are confirmed by measured DNA. Of those only gradient boosting flags, 33 of 121 (27%) are confirmed, a weaker but real set. Of those only the linear model flags, 0 of 8 are confirmed. As a baseline, 5 of 67 (7%) knockouts that neither model flags shift anyway.

Why it matters. A label-free screen can be mined for cell-cycle regulators, and the hits hold up against a direct DNA measurement.

7Some expected arrests did not happen, and phase contrast was right about that

The team listed 60 genes expected to stop cells in G1, S or G2/M. Measured DNA agrees with the S-phase group and contradicts the G2/M group.

What we found. S-phase genes gain 4N cells (median +4.7 points). G1 genes gain 2N cells (+6.1 points), though few are significant one by one. The mitotic and checkpoint genes expected to pile up in G2/M lose 4N cells instead (median -2.5 points). They are not hiding as cells with two nuclei either (10.0% against 10.4% in controls); only KIF23 clearly is (31%).

A hypothesis we tested. Brian proposed that G1-arrested cells keep growing until they look like G2 cells. Knockout cells with one genome copy are indeed larger than control cells in 148 of 158 knockouts, but they are not called 4N more often, and a DNA floor on the 4N call changes no knockout by more than 0.63 points.

Why it matters. Literature expectations for a gene do not always hold in a given cell line and time window (here about 89 hours of Cas9). A direct readout is needed to know.

Brian's updated panels

What we did. Brian revised the expected outcome for each group of genes and redrew the knockout panels on the corrected clock labels (4N at 0.5 to 0.75, just-divided cells at 0.75 to 1), each against groups of control cells of the same size. We put the measured DNA of the same knockouts next to them (about 200 cells each).

What we found. The replication and cytokinesis genes move as expected, and measured DNA moves the same way. CCNB1 shows no clear shift on the clock, and its guides disagree with each other (next part). BUB1B gains early-G1 cells as expected, but its DNA distribution does not change. Slippage out of mitosis would leave G1 cells with doubled DNA, so the gain more likely reflects a shorter mitosis once the checkpoint is gone.

Guides of the same gene can disagree

What Louise found. Each gene is targeted by four guide RNAs. In CCNB1, MCM3 and CENPC the expected arrest is not clear at the gene level, but the guides of each gene differ (p = 0.016, 0.046 and 0.027). Two CCNB1 guides add about 15 points of G2/M cells while another adds 12 points of G1 cells, so the gene average hides both. The guide ranking holds up in two separate sets of cells scored by different readouts (G1 fraction, rank correlation 0.82). All three genes also carry more just-divided cells than controls (20 to 26% against 13%). That shift is shared rather than gene-specific, and may be a general response to cutting.

The same question on measured DNA. For the 111 newly measured knockouts (median 4 guides each, 32 cells in the smallest), we compared the guides' 2N, S and 4N mix with control guides of the same sizes, so ordinary guide-to-guide variation is part of the reference. The guides differ more than control guides in 9 knockouts at p < 0.05 (about 6 expected by chance) and in 0 after correcting for testing many knockouts. Among the confirmed knockouts, 114 of 118 guides move 4N cells in the knockout's direction, and all guides agree in 26 of 30 knockouts. With about 50 cells per guide, this test only sees large differences between guides.

Why it matters. For most knockouts the guides agree, so gene-level calls are sound. Where a gene's expected arrest is missing, as for CCNB1, check its guides one by one: guide efficiency varies, and a gene average can hide guides that push in opposite directions.

8Removing the cycle tightens a few main axes but barely changes heterogeneity

The cycle concentrates in the strongest axes of variation, so those shrink noticeably. Over all features it is a few percent, and perturbed populations stay almost as varied as before.

What we did. Diego removed the measured clock position from control-cell profiles and compared the variation within each image field before and after. We repeated this on cells from all 1,000 knockouts and on Element, and asked how much each knockout's shift comes from changing the cycle mix versus changing the cells at the same cycle stage.

What we found. The top principal components (the main axes of variation) tighten by 26 to 33% in 4i and 9 to 19% in phase contrast, but a typical single feature loses about 1% of its variance (median ratio 0.989 in 4i, 0.993 in phase contrast; a tail of a few hundred features loses 10 to 35%), and differences between fields and wells barely change. Knockout populations become 0.6 to 5.5% tighter and separate from controls just as well as before. Of 1,000 knockouts, 790 change the cells at a matched cycle stage, 80 change both, and only 1 acts through the cycle mix alone.

Why it matters. Correcting for the cycle is cheap and tightens the dominant axes, but it is not the main source of single-cell heterogeneity. Field effects, clonal patches and local cell density matter more.

9With RNA as ground truth, imaging reads the cycle except just after division

In the Element data, images predict the RNA-based clock to a typical error of 37.5 degrees in wells the model never saw (a shuffled clock gives 77.9).

What we found. The DNA stain carries most of the signal, and the phospho-antibodies add some. Images fail on one stretch, just after division: the DNA is back to one copy while the RNA still looks like G2/M. The largest image changes around the cycle are at division, where phospho-p38 and phospho-ERK rise and nuclei shrink.

Knockout-level RNA. The CROP-seq data, averaged per knockout, carry little cell-cycle signal: 14 of 997 knockouts move a cell-cycle gene programme strongly, and agreement with the imaging readout is weak (rank correlation about 0.1).

Why it matters. RNA and images measure different moments of the same cycle. Single-cell paired data are what make a cell-level comparison possible.

10Take-home messages

  1. Label-free phase contrast is a usable cell-cycle readout, confirmed against a DNA stain in hundreds of knockouts.
  2. The cell cycle is a small part of single-cell variation (3 to 9%). Removing it tightens a few main axes and leaves knockout phenotypes and field effects mostly in place.
  3. The cycle is more useful as a readout: which perturbations shift it, and what they change in cells at the same stage.
  4. Anchor any learned clock to measured DNA, and compare datasets through DNA-content classes rather than angles.

Limits. One cell line and one screen; a measured clock for about two thirds of control cells; predicted, not measured, clocks for most knockout cells; across datasets only the S to G2/M stretch aligns.

Next. Every knockout either model flags now has measured DNA. Next: more cells per guide for the knockouts whose guides disagree, the 4i markers for knockout cells (Diego's questions 2 and 3), anchors beyond matching feature names for the cross-dataset transfer, and image embeddings (Cell-DINO) as the phase-contrast input.

Words used on this page

2N, S, 4N
One genome copy (G1), copying DNA, two copies (G2 and mitosis). Measured from the total DNA stain in the nucleus.
Phase contrast
A label-free microscope image that shows cell and nuclear outlines and texture without any stain.
4i
Iterative indirect immunofluorescence imaging: the same cells are stained, imaged and stripped repeatedly to read many antibodies.
pRb, Rb, p21
Phosphorylated Rb rises when a cell commits to divide; p21 holds cells back in G1.
Optical pooled screen
Many CRISPR knockouts grown together in one well; each cell's knockout is read from a barcode in the image.
Guide RNA
The 20-letter sequence that directs Cas9 to a gene. Each gene here has four, and they can differ in how well they knock the gene out.
Non-targeting control
Cells with a guide RNA that cuts nowhere; the reference for every knockout.
Held out
Tested on image tiles or wells the model never saw during training.
AUC
The chance that a random 4N cell gets a higher score than a random 2N cell. 0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect.
Rank correlation
Spearman rho: how well two lists agree in order, from -1 to 1.
Confirmed
Significant against groups of control cells of the same size, after correcting for testing many knockouts (false discovery rate 5%).
Principal component
One of the main axes along which cells vary in a feature space.
Removing the cycle
Subtracting, from every feature, the part that follows clock position.
